content: Hair-grooming syncope, also referred to as hair-combing syncope, is a specific type of fainting disorder that occurs during activities such as combing or brushing one’s hair. This condition is most commonly observed in children between the ages of five and sixteen. The clinical presentation of hair-grooming syncope typically begins with presyncopal symptoms during hair-related activities, including combing, brushing, braiding, trimming, curling, or blow-drying. These symptoms are often followed by a sudden loss of consciousness and, in some cases, convulsions. Additional symptoms that may occur before or after the syncopal episode include migraines, abdominal pain, a sensation of feeling funny, or blurred vision. The underlying causes of this condition are thought to involve pain or nerve stimulation on the scalp, which is similar to the mechanism seen in parade-ground syncope. Another possible cause is the compression of blood vessels or nerves due to neck flexion or extension during hair grooming activities. A 2009 study identified 111 pediatric cases of hair-grooming syncope in the United States. Approximately three-quarters of these cases involved female patients. The study also noted that in males, the condition was most commonly associated with hair cutting, whereas in females, it was more frequently linked to hair brushing. Hair-grooming syncope is sometimes misdiagnosed as epilepsy. However, it is more accurately classified as a paroxysmal non-epileptic event. It may also have a potential association with orthostatic hypotension. Importantly, this condition is not linked to any abnormalities of the heart. This form of syncope has been proposed as a possible explanation for the extremely rare phenomenon known as hair-brushing syndrome. In this syndrome, static electricity is hypothesized to disrupt brain or organ function. To date, only two cases of hair-brushing syndrome have been reported worldwide. One of these cases gained media attention in 2011 when the Daily Mail published a report suggesting that hair brushing could potentially lead to death.
